readerTitle: Webvan and Instacart: same idea, different decade
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Webvan, Instacart) + 가상 적용 (동네 식당, 소프트웨어 아이디어 3개)
insight: 좋은 아이디어인지보다 '무엇이 바뀌었길래 지금 가능한가'를 먼저 묻는다. 같은 아이디어도 시기에 따라 실패와 성공이 갈린다.
misconception: 아직 아무도 안 했다면 기회다. 고객이 원하기만 하면 언제 시작하든 상관없다.

sources.text: Webvan 파산 신청 보도 (2001년 7월), 예: The New York Times, CNET 기사
Webvan과 Bechtel의 물류창고 건설 계약 보도 (1999년)
Instacart 회사 소개 및 창업 관련 보도 (2012년 샌프란시스코 창업)

factChecks.note: Webvan: 1999년 샌프란시스코 베이 지역에서 서비스 시작, 대형 자동화 물류창고 구축, 2001년 7월 파산 신청. 날짜를 게시 전 다시 확인하세요. 투자 유치 금액은 자료마다 달라 카드에는 "hundreds of millions of dollars"로만 적었습니다.
Instacart: 2012년 창업, 기존 매장에서 쇼퍼가 대신 장을 보는 방식, 자체 창고 없음. 창업 연도와 초기 모델 설명을 확인하세요.
"the iPhone was eight years away": iPhone 출시 2007년 − 1999년 = 8년. 계산 확인.
Webvan 실패 원인은 시기만이 아니라 과도한 확장과 고정비도 큽니다. 7번 카드에서 이 점을 밝혔습니다. 원인을 하나로 단정하지 않도록 문구를 검토하세요.

cards.title: Webvan and Instacart: same idea, different decade
body: In 1999, Webvan let people order groceries online and have them delivered at home. By 2001, it had filed for bankruptcy.
In 2012, Instacart launched with almost the same promise. It grew into one of the best-known delivery businesses in North America.

image.label: Two grocery bags, one labeled 1999 and one labeled 2012
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 문 앞에 놓인 장바구니 두 개. 왼쪽은 "1999" 태그와 옆에 데스크톱 컴퓨터·전화선, 오른쪽은 "2012" 태그와 옆에 스마트폰. 실제 회사 로고와 브랜드 색은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's 1999. Would you back grocery delivery?
body: A team pitches you online grocery ordering with home delivery. Surveys say busy families love the idea. They plan to build large warehouses in many cities.
Before you invest, which question matters most?

options.feedback: Worth asking, and the answer was mostly yes. But wanting something isn't enough if ordering it is still slow and awkward for most people.

options.text: What has changed that makes this work now and not five years ago?
options.feedback: This tests whether the world is ready, not just whether the idea is nice. In 1999 the honest answer was thin.

options.text: Can they build warehouses fast enough to beat copycats?
options.feedback: Speed matters once the timing is right. If it isn't, moving fast just burns money faster.

cards.title: Webvan was early, and it bet big.
body: In 1999, few homes had fast internet. Ordering meant sitting at a desktop computer. The iPhone was eight years away.
Webvan raised hundreds of millions of dollars and built costly automated warehouses. Those warehouses needed lots of orders to pay off. The orders didn't come fast enough.
By 2012, most shoppers carried a smartphone. Instacart didn't build warehouses. Shoppers picked groceries from stores that already existed, guided by an app.

cards.title: Why now?
body: **Why now** is the change in the world that makes an idea possible, cheap enough or wanted at this moment, when it wasn't before.
A good idea with no recent change behind it raises a hard question: if it's so good, why hasn't it already worked? A clear *why now* answers that question.

image.label: A closed door in 1999 and an open door in 2012
image.brief: 같은 문이 두 번 그려진 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "1999"는 닫혀 있고, 오른쪽 "2012"는 열려 있음. 열린 문 앞에 "Smartphones", "Shoppers used to apps" 라벨이 붙은 열쇠들.

cards.title: Four kinds of change open doors.
body: Most strong answers to *why now* point to one of these:
list: **Technology:** something becomes possible, like ordering from a phone
**Cost:** something gets cheap enough, like card readers small vendors can afford
**Behavior:** people start doing something new, like paying with their phones
**Rules:** a law or standard changes what's allowed
cards.callout: The change should be recent, real and hard to undo.

cards.title: It works for a corner restaurant too.
body: You're thinking of opening a lunch spot. The food is good, but so is the place two streets over.

Then you learn a large office building opens nearby next spring, with hundreds of workers and no canteen. That's a *why now*. It explains why this street, this year, can support a new lunch place when it couldn't before.
Without that change, you're just competing for the same customers.

image.label: A new office tower beside a small restaurant
image.brief: 거리 풍경 일러스트. 공사 막바지인 새 오피스 빌딩 옆에 작은 점심 식당. 빌딩에서 사람들이 쏟아져 나오는 점선 화살표가 식당 쪽으로. 실제 상호나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Timing is one reason, not the only one.
body: Webvan also spent heavily before demand was proven. Instacart also chose a cheaper model. Timing helped, but choices mattered too.

And being early looks a lot like being wrong. You can't control when a change spreads. A *why now* story that depends on a trend "about to take off" is a guess, so plan for it taking longer than you hope.

cards.title: Three software pitches. Which has the best why now?
body: Three founders want to build software for small accounting firms. Each explains why the time is right.

options.feedback: That may mean an open field, or it may mean others tried and it didn't work. It doesn't say what changed.
Size tells you the prize is big, not why it's winnable today rather than years ago.

options.text: "Most of these firms moved their files online in the last two years, so tools can now connect to them cheaply."
options.feedback: It names a recent, real change that makes the product easier to build and adopt. You can check it by asking firms.

cards.title: Ask what changed, not just whether it's good.
body: A strong idea names the recent change that makes it work today.
**Try it today:** take your current idea or plan. Finish this sentence in one line: "This works now, and didn't five years ago, because…"
